item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — The Dodgers can only hope it looks this good in October.
One night after Tarik Skubal went seven innings in his first scoreless outing as a Dodger, Yoshinobu Yamamoto matched him, allowing only one hit in his seven scoreless innings as the Dodgers shut out the Cincinnati Reds, 4-0, on Tuesday night.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going tomorrow – you feel good about preventing runs,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
The win moved the Dodgers (92-59) within one day of clinching their 13th NL West division title in the past 14 seasons. Their magic number is one after the second-place San Diego Padres (82-69) lost to the Colorado Rockies later Tuesday night.
The Dodgers’ lead over the Atlanta Braves (89-63) for the No. 2 seed in the National League remains 3½ games. Their magic number to clinch a first-round bye is eight.
All of that makes the final two weeks of the regular season a chance for the Dodgers to get things right for October and their three-peat pursuit. The starting rotation appears to be there already.
Skubal has a 1.73 ERA over his past four starts. With Tuesday’s outing, Yamamoto’s ERA is 1.79 over his past seven starts. Blake Snell starts on Wednesday – and he has given up a total of only four runs in six starts since returning from elbow surgery. Only fourth starter Tyler Glasnow (eight runs in 10 innings over his past two starts) seems to have some work to do before being October-ready.
“Yeah, pretty good,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said after his first three-hit game since Aug. 17. “You have Blake Snell going tomorrow. Tyler on the back end of that too. Roki’s on his way back.
“It’s a special pitching staff. It really is. So as an offense, we just need to score a few runs for them, just like we did last year.”
Yamamoto started Tuesday by giving the Reds hope – he walked the first two batters he faced – then he took it away, retiring 21 of the next 22 batters he faced.
“They took a little moment for me,” Yamamoto said through his interpreter of the mound visit from catcher Hunter Feduccia and pitching coach Mark Prior that followed the walks. “They came up to me and, ‘Hey, how you doing?’ and just checked in on me. And then I was able to get back to my normal rhythm.”
Elly De La Cruz had the only hit off Yamamoto, a double into the left-field corner with two outs in the third inning.
But even that was a victory – Yamamoto kept him in the ballpark after De La Cruz had hit a home run in each of the previous four games between the Dodgers and Reds. He then retired the next 13 batters in order, getting six of his seven strikeouts.
“After the first two hitters, it was vintage Yama,” Roberts said. “Just attacking, not trying to be too fine. Not giving these guys too much credit. And yeah, at first, it didn’t look promising as far as pitch count, the two walks. But then he kind of dialed things in, like he’s been known to do.”
The Dodgers gave him a lead in the second inning when Max Muncy was hit by a pitch and Tommy Edman and Hunter Feduccia followed with singles. They added to it in the third inning with a two-run home run from Teoscar Hernandez, who remains hot – 24 for 63 (.381) in his past 18 games.
“It’s been very helpful,” Roberts said of Hernandez’s late-season renaissance. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. The last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him. The defense ticked up. The at-bat quality, the taking walks, all of it. I can’t say enough about what he’s done the last 10 days.”
De La Cruz had another hit, a single in the ninth inning that put runners on the corners for the Reds with no outs. Tanner Scott struck out Sal Stewart, Jose Trevino and Eugenio Suarez to close out the shutout.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] How Tarik Skubal found ‘who I know I am’ in Dodgers adjustment process
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI –– Every day, Tarik Skubal learns something new about playing for the Dodgers.
Monday's lesson: Clinching a playoff spot warrants only subtle celebrations.
"It's different than anything I've experienced, for sure," Skubal chuckled on Monday night, after the Dodgers recognized their 14th consecutive postseason berth with only a subdued postgame champagne toast and brief speech from manager Dave Roberts.
"But," the club's new star pitcher added, "I think it just speaks to the people in this room and what they expect out of this team. That was cool. A little toast and move on. Forget it happened. We've got more to accomplish this season."
Consider it the latest step in Skubal's acclimation process with the Dodgers –– another little moment that made him feel more at home with his new team.
He's now six weeks on from his emotional trade from the Detroit Tigers at the deadline.
And he's starting to find a comfort level that, after an uneven start to his Dodgers tenure, is helping him look more like the star pitcher he is accustomed to being.
"Constantly learning each other and developing relationships –– a lot of that stuff you don't realize, no one writes about that kind of relationship –– but I think it matters, it matters a lot. I probably underestimated that a little bit," said Skubal, who had spent the entirety of his career in Detroit before his marquee move to the Dodgers.
"But just communicating, having an open dialogue with everyone, all these guys, on what I like to do, what I'm comfortable with and honestly what I'm uncomfortable with … I think we're developing a real good relationship," he added.
And as a result, as manager Dave Roberts noted, "I think the last couple [outings he has made] have been his best."
That was certainly true on Monday, when Skubal spun a gem with the Dodgers' postseason berth in the balance.
He delivered his first scoreless start with the team by blanking the Reds over seven innings at Great American Ball Park. He gave up just three hits and one walk while striking out nine batters in a 90-pitch domination.
"To take the mound on the night that we had a chance to clinch, and we did it," Roberts said, "I think that's something he should be proud of."
More important to Skubal was the way it reflected his growing familiarity with the Dodgers' catchers and pitching department.
He noted he only shook Will Smith off one time all night. He praised the rhythm he has developed with pitching coaches in pre-game prep meetings. And he credited it all with helping him eliminate some perfectionist tendencies that hampered his first month with the team (when he gave up nine runs in 24 innings while lacking the ruthless efficiency that made him a reigning back-to-back Cy Young Award winner).
"I think a lot of the struggles have been 'me vs. me,' thinking too much out there and not competing the way I know how to compete," Skubal said. "Sometimes I try to be too perfect with things instead of just attacking guys over the middle of the plate and letting my stuff play, especially early in games, behind in the count, just not trying to be too fine."
To put it more simply, Skubal added, it was a process of "trying to find the rhythm of who I know I am."
And to people around the team, it's no coincidence that has happened as he's carved out a place in his new clubhouse, as well.
"He's just chill," pitching coach Mark Prior said. "You can joke around with him. You can talk to him."
Few players have grown closer with Skubal than Blake Snell to this point. They've sat side-by-side in the dugout during games, locked in constant conversation. They were pulling practical jokes on one another Tuesday, knocking over each other's chairs in the clubhouse. They've even begun making Step Brothers-inspired jokes about being new best friends on social media.
"I think we're best friends," Snell deadpanned. "Some days, he agrees."
Snell told the California Post that their relationship blossomed naturally, with Snell immediately being struck by how Skubal was "very confident and very secure with who he is" even amid new surroundings.
Two other observations:
"I didn't think he was that funny," Snell joked, describing a side of Skubal that came out Monday night when he razzed backup catcher Hunter Feduccia about a snazzy short-sleeve dress shirt and matching pair of brown slacks ("Outfit of the day!" Skubal declared).
"And," Snell added, "I like how competitive he is. Because it just makes both of us so much better."
That latter dynamic could fuel the Dodgers' entire rotation moving forward, especially entering a postseason in which the group will likely have to carry the team.
"Every time one of our boys go, we want them to dominate, and then the next man up wants to do even better," Snell said. "I think that's very important, to know that we're supporting each other and we're pushing each other to be great, and that we're not focused on just our own achievements. We're focused on our group of starting pitchers all succeeding."
Prior echoed those sentiments, noting that with Skubal specifically: "He wants to have fun. And he wants to win."
Lately, Skubal has been, now on a four-start stretch with only five runs allowed in his last 26 innings.
For the Dodgers, it's a sign of his growth process since being acquired by the club; one that could prove crucial in their three-peat ambitions.
"It's hard to get in that rhythm [and develop] that trust," Roberts said. "But for me, I see just more of the trust in whatever is called, and then you can just go out there [be himself]."
